intent: A country that lost its coast in a war it still refuses to accept, told as a map: the shore it had, the war that took it, the court that said no, and the lake where its sailors train today.
pacing_profile: documentary: cold open, place, why in 2–5 beats, twist, close answers the open, short CTA (docs/STORY_GUIDELINES.md §2)
pause_policy: Pause only at the marked ellipses.
title: The navy with no sea

lines.direction: the opening line, cold — the map is already moving
lines.text: Bolivia has a navy. It has not had a coastline for more than a century.

lines.direction: draw the coast as it is named; pin the port
lines.text: This is the Pacific shore Bolivia once held, a long desert coast around Antofagasta.

lines.direction: Chile lights solid on its name; the coast route recolours into Chile; Bolivia pulses on landlocked
lines.text: In 1879 Chile marched north in the War of the Pacific. Within a few years the coast was Chilean, and Bolivia was landlocked.

lines.direction: pull back to the whole country; flag sticker on the Day of the Sea; the court card lands on lost
lines.text: Bolivia never accepted it. Every March it marks the Day of the Sea, with parades far from any shore, and in 2018 it took Chile to the World Court, asking for a way back to the ocean. It lost.

lines.direction: the twist: tighten onto the lake; the lake glows; the pin and the counter on sailors
lines.text: So where does the navy sail? Up here, on Lake Titicaca, nearly 4 kilometres up in the Andes, with around 5,000 sailors and a fleet of patrol boats.

lines.direction: answer the opening line with the same noun
lines.text: A navy without a sea, drilling on a mountain lake, waiting for a coast it still calls its own.

lines.direction: short follow — the outro visual does the work
lines.text: Follow for a new map story every day.
